cse-2003-cs-66.approach: The input has only $\Theta(\log n)$ bits. Binary search for $m$ in $[0,n]$ takes $O(\log n)$ rounds, each cubing an $O(\log n)$-bit number — polylogarithmic. Writing the $\approx\tfrac13\log n$-bit answer already needs $\Omega(\log n)$ time.

steps.title: Upper bound
steps.body: Binary search over $[0,n]$: $\lceil\log_2(n+1)\rceil$ iterations. Each computes $m^3$ with $m$ of $O(\log n)$ bits: $O((\log n)^2)$ by schoolbook multiplication. Total $O((\log n)^3)$, i.e. $O((\log n)^k)$ with $k=3$.

steps.title: Lower bound
steps.body: The answer $m\approx n^{1/3}$ has about $\tfrac13\log_2 n$ bits, and all must be written (and the input read). So time is $\Omega(\log n)$, which is not $O((\log\log n)^m)$ for any constant $m$.

answer.value: $O((\log n)^k)$ for some $k>0$, but not $O((\log\log n)^m)$ for any $m>0$

optionAnalysis.reason: $O(n)$ is a gross overestimate; polylog time suffices, so "not $O(n^{0.5})$" is false.
False: it **is** $O((\log n)^k)$.
Correct.
Impossible: the output alone has $\Theta(\log n)$ bits.

cse-2003-cs-66.verification: Example: $n=2^{30}$ (31 bits) — binary search needs about 31 rounds of cubing 31-bit numbers, nowhere near $\sqrt{n}=2^{15}$ steps.

cse-2003-cs-67.approach: A path from $v_1$ has cost 0 exactly when it uses only $E_1$ edges. So the computed costs reveal which vertices of $V_1$ are reachable inside $G_1$ — i.e. whether $G_1$ is connected.

steps.title: Meaning of cost 0
steps.body: Every edge of $E_1$ has weight 0, others weight 1. $d(v_1,v)=0$ iff there is a $v_1$–$v$ path using only $E_1$ edges, i.e. $v$ is in $v_1$'s component of $G_1$.

steps.title: Inference
steps.body: $G_1$ is connected $\iff d(v_1,v)=0$ for every $v\in V_1$. Both directions follow from step 1, so connectivity of $G_1$ can always be read off the costs.

optionAnalysis.reason: Costs count only non-$E_1$ edges; zero-weight edges are invisible, so edge counts are lost.
Correct.
Costs cannot reveal whether every pair of $V_1$ is directly joined.
Whether $G_1$ has cycles (extra zero edges) does not change any distance.

cse-2003-cs-67.verification: Two graphs with the same $V_1$ but $E_1$ a path vs. a cycle give identical costs — so tree-ness (D) and clique-ness (C) are not determined, while connectivity is.

cse-2003-cs-68.approach: Kruskal: take edges in increasing weight, skipping any that closes a cycle; stop after $10-1=9$ edges.

steps.title: Weights 1 and 2
steps.body: Take $a\text{–}c$ (1), $a\text{–}d$ (2), $b\text{–}h$ (2), $e\text{–}i$ (2). Skip $c\text{–}d$ (2): $c,d$ already joined via $a$. Running total $1+2+2+2=7$.

steps.title: Weights 3, 4, 5
steps.body: Take $b\text{–}d$ (3), $g\text{–}i$ (4), $g\text{–}f$ (4), $j\text{–}i$ (5). Total $7+3+4+4+5=23$. Components now: $\{a,b,c,d,h\}$ and $\{e,f,g,i,j\}$.

steps.title: Join the two halves
steps.body: Skip $a\text{–}b$ (6, cycle). The cheapest edge between the components has weight 8 ($a\text{–}e$ or $h\text{–}g$); take one. Total $23+8=31$; 9 edges, done. Remaining edges ($f\text{–}i$ 9, $e\text{–}f$ 11, …) all close cycles.

optionAnalysis.reason: 29 would need a connecting edge of weight 6 between the two halves; none exists.
38 includes a costlier, non-minimal connecting edge (e.g. $d\text{–}g$ 15).
41 is far above the Kruskal total.

pitfalls: Some weights in the scanned figure are hard to read; the total is unaffected by the $a\text{–}d$ label (2 or 7) since $c\text{–}d$ (2) serves equally.
cse-2003-cs-68.verification: Cut check: the cut $\{a,b,c,d,h\}$ vs $\{e,f,g,i,j\}$ is crossed by $a\text{–}e$ 8, $h\text{–}g$ 8, $h\text{–}i$ 14, $d\text{–}g$ 15, $h\text{–}j$ 19 — the light edge is 8. Inside each side the chosen edges are the cheapest spanning ones (sums $1+2+2+3=8$ and $2+4+4+5=15$), and $8+15+8=31$.

cse-2003-cs-69.approach: Minimum rooms = maximum number of activities in progress at the same moment (interval-graph colouring). Sweep the events: +1 at a start, −1 at an end, and take the peak.

steps.title: Peak
steps.body: The maximum is 4, right after $f_s$: $b,d,e,f$ are all running. So at least 4 rooms are needed, and the greedy assignment (reuse any freed room) achieves 4.

optionAnalysis.reason: 3 rooms cannot hold $b,d,e,f$, which overlap just after $f_s$.
Correct: the peak overlap is 4.
5 exceeds the peak; greedy room reuse needs only 4.
6 is far above the peak overlap.

pitfalls: The scanned reprint drops $c_e$ from the event list; with $c$ never ending the peak would be 5. The original paper lists $c_e$ after $d_s$.
